text.p: India's cotton exports in 1996/97 (October/September) are expected to be higher at 1.4 million bales (one bale is 170 kg) compared to 790,000 bales in the previous season, traders said on Thursday.
"This is mainly because of the spillover of about 400,000 bales from the previous year which has been shipped during the current season," said a trader.

India has authorised an export quota of 1.34 million bales for the current season. Of this, 1.15 million bales cotton has been registered and the actual shipments till July-end amounted to 900,000 bales.
Traders they would expect at least 100,000 bales out of the remaining 250,000 bales to be shipped before the end of the current season.
Total shipments, including the spillover, would be about 1.4 million bales, the traders added.
A report by the U.S. agricultural attache based in New Delhi confirms traders estimates.
The report, released on Wednesday said India's cotton exports through July 23 totaled 1.3 million bales, including 395,645 bales of spillover from 1995/96 export quotas.
Meanwhile, cotton prices on the Bombay market rose on limited supply despite poor buying from mills in the week to Thursday, dealers said.
"But speculative buying has triggered a rise in prices as traders reported a shortage of ready stock," said Mahesh Thakkar, a leading cotton dealer.
Thakkar said most mills had enough stocks to last up to three months which could see them through the current season, ending September.
Dealers said cotton supplies had remained thin as the 1996/97 season headed towards end.
They said the bulk of the current season's cotton crop, estimated at 17 million bales (one bale is 170 kg) had been marketed.
"There is not much cotton left in the market," said Thakkar. "Widespread rains have also hampered transportation of cotton from producing centres to market places."
"There is also an acute shortage of good quality cotton," Thakkar said.
In the week to Thursday, spot Bengal-deshi rose 55 rupees to 1,060/1,120 rupees per maund (37.32 kg). Punjab F-414 gained 10 rupees to 2,070/2,090 rupees per maund.
Gujarat Kalyan cotton rose 100 rupees to 14,200/14,700 rupees per candy (355.56 kg) and Wagad made a similar gain at 13,000/13,200 rupees per candy.
